extraction.name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
extraction.description: An object hallucination evaluation dataset and method for large vision-language models. POPE constructs triples containing an image, multiple questions about the presence of objects, and Yes/No answers. Evaluation questions use random, popular, or adversarial sampling of nonexistent objects, with a 1:1 ratio of present and nonexistent objects. The paper evaluates POPE on MSCOCO and extends it to A-OKVQA and GQA using automatic segmentation.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3 [cs.CV], 26 October 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: For the initial CHAIR evaluation, the authors randomly sampled 2,000 images with object annotations and human-labeled captions from the MSCOCO validation set. For annotation-based POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly selected 500 validation images with more than three ground-truth objects in their annotations and constructed six questions per image. They also used SEEM to annotate images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA and constructed POPE questions from the segmentation results.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images, object annotations, and human-labeled captions from the MSCOCO validation set; images from A-OKVQA and GQA. For automatically annotated variants, object labels were obtained from SEEM segmentation results.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images and object labels were converted into image-question-answer triples using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'. Present and nonexistent objects were included in a 1:1 ratio. Random sampling selects objects absent from the image at random. Popular sampling selects the most frequent objects in the whole image dataset that are absent from the current image. Adversarial sampling ranks objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and selects the highest-ranked absent objects.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For annotation-based MSCOCO POPE, images were restricted to those with more than three annotated ground-truth objects, and 500 images were randomly selected. For automatically annotated variants, SEEM segmentation was used to obtain objects before constructing questions. The separate CHAIR evaluation considered only the 80 object categories in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth objects were obtained either from existing human annotations or from automatic segmentation using SEEM. Questions about ground-truth objects were assigned 'Yes' answers, while questions about sampled nonexistent objects were assigned 'No' answers. Six questions were constructed per image in the annotation-based MSCOCO evaluation, with equal proportions of Yes and No labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors compared SEEM-based POPE with POPE using human ground-truth annotations. Model rankings and the Random > Popular > Adversarial performance trend were mostly consistent, but evaluation scores differed. They attributed differences to the finer granularity of SEEM segmentation results and noted that the segmentation tool's label set may be inconsistent with human annotations.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that object hallucination can degrade model performance, harm user experiences, and hinder safe real-world deployment. It gives autonomous driving as an example where incorrect understanding of the environment could lead to wrong decisions and serious safety issues. The evaluation is intended to support the development of more reliable and human-aligned large vision-language models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper describes MSCOCO-based visual instruction datasets as having an unbalanced object distribution in which frequently occurring objects occupy a major portion of the data. It finds that models are more likely to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with those present in an image. POPE's popular and adversarial sampling settings explicitly target these object distributions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: POPE focuses on coarse-grained object presence and does not evaluate fine-grained hallucinations involving object counts, attributes, or positions. Its scores do not measure overall model capability. Computational constraints limited evaluation to subsets of each dataset's validation data, and results may be affected by those subsets' distributions. Matching-based interpretation of model Yes/No responses can be inaccurate when responses do not explicitly contain those words. Automatic segmentation labels may differ from human annotations and produce divergent evaluation results. The study evaluated only a small number of models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models through binary object-presence questions. Random, popular, and adversarial settings provide different evaluation difficulty levels. Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 score are reported, with F1 as the principal metric and the proportion of Yes responses used to analyze model behavior. Automatic segmentation allows extension to datasets without object annotations. Higher POPE scores should not be interpreted as stronger overall model capability.
